full_judgment: 6. The difficulty in deciding this point straight away on the basis of the aforesaid established principle of law has arisen because of a new trend of decision of the Supreme Court of India. Their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India are now of the opinion that in order to enable a person to make a demand for preemption by way of Talab-i-Mowasibat under Muslim Law one will have to wait till the completion of the sale i.e. the completion of all formalities as contemplated under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act and section 61 of the Registration Act. This major departure on this principle of law in the subcontinent for the first time took place through a decision reported in A.I.R. 1960 (S.C.) 1368. Although the said decision considered the earlier decisions on this point reported in I.L.R. 7 All I.L.R. 16 All and A.I.R. 1923 (PC) it did not assign any specific reason as to what impelled their Lordships to differ with the time honored principle of law as finally approved by the Privy Council. Their Lordships instead straight away held that a sale of property is complete when all the formalities under section 54 of Transfer of Property Act and section 61 of the Registration Act are complete and not before and earlier. In a subsequent decision reported in A.I.R. 1961 (SC) 1747 this point again came up for consideration in detail when out of five judges, three judgment affirmed the aforesaid decision reported in A.I.R 1950 (SC) 1368. The two judges who delivered a dissenting judgment held that since once the registration of a document it complete under section 61 of the Registration Act, it takes effect from the date of execution of the document under section 47 of the Registration Act, it must be held that a from demand for pre-emption by way of Talab-i-Mowasibat can be made before the completion of registration but after execution. The dissenting judgment of the judges of the Supreme Court of India as referred to hereinbefore is based on the reasons that Talab-i-Mowasibat being first demand for preemption requires to be made immediately on receiving information's of the sale; after registration of the deed of sale under section 61 of the Registration Act, the effect of such sale having taken place from the date of execution under section 47 of the Registration Act, it is quite proper that the first demand for preemption can be made at any time between the execution and registration of the deed of sale. The difficulty in making the first demand for preemption by way of Talab-I-Mawasibat immediately on receiving information of the sale but after the registration is posed in the dissenting judgment of their Lordships in A.I.R. 1961 (SC) 1747. This was also carefully taken note of by the Supreme Court of India in a much later decision reported in AIR 1972 (SC) 2162.
